A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DDA study, and their text, equations, tables and figures are readable and matchable. The supplied v1 ends with references and contains no appendix; v4 includes Appendices A–F. The supplied material supports a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original detector evaluations in Tables 3–9, reconstruction and timing measurements, robustness experiments and ablations.

after.justification: v4 retains those original results and adds benchmark evaluations, configuration ablations, feature-space comparisons and regional detection analyses in its appendix.

M1.justification: DDA retains VAE reconstruction, high-frequency DCT coefficient replacement and pixel mixup, with the same equations and DINOv2 detector using rank-8 LoRA. The appendix tests alternative configurations but introduces no new component into the proposed DDA method.

E1.justification: Appendix C adds ForenSynth and AIGCDetectionBenchmark to the original eight benchmarks. Despite overlap with existing generators, these evaluations substantially broaden represented generator populations, including CycleGAN, ProGAN, StyleGAN, CRN, IMLE and DeepFake outputs. The original training source and EvalGEN generator coverage remain unchanged.

E2.justification: v1 includes B-Free in detection-accuracy comparisons only on WildRF. v4 Table 14 adds B-Free to a Synthbuster comparison, using results attributed to the B-Free paper. The comparator membership in the retained main-text experiments is unchanged.

E3.justification: Added experiments introduce JPEG-96 preprocessing for the new benchmarks, a five-generator Synthbuster comparison using multiple-crop logit averaging, input-size trials from 224 to 504, and linear-probing versus LoRA backbone comparisons. Mixed-VAE training is also evaluated. These substantially expand evaluation protocols; Appendix A's newly disclosed default training settings do not establish changes to existing experiments.

E4.justification: v1 already contains frequency-threshold, pixel-mixing and VAE ablations plus compression, resizing and blur robustness tests. v4 retains them and adds input-size and backbone/training-strategy ablations, mixed-VAE analysis, feature-separation comparisons across detectors and regional-score heatmaps (Tables 15–17; Figures 11 and 13). These investigate substantial additional questions about sensitivity, learnability and artifact localization.

E5.justification: Both versions report descriptive means and standard deviations across evaluation subsets and variation in reconstruction/timing measurements. The appendix extends the existing reporting convention to additional results. It adds no repeated-training run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance-testing procedures.

E6.justification: Tables 1–10 and the original robustness and ablation plots retain their results. Tables 11–17 add substantial results, including reported DDA means of 93.3 on AIGCDetectionBenchmark and 85.5 on ForenSynth, where C2P-CLIP (92.1) and FatFormer (90.1) rank higher. Table 14's 99.0 Synthbuster result uses a different generator subset and crop-aggregation protocol from Table 7's 94.6, so it is not a same-setting improvement.

T1.justification: The reconstruction equations and pixel-mixup definition remain unchanged. No new formal assumptions, theorems, proofs or derivations appear. The added decision-boundary illustration supplies conceptual explanation rather than new mathematical results.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central claims about frequency bias after reconstruction, DDA's generalization benefits and the contributions of DDA-COCO and EvalGEN. Their headline eight-benchmark claims also remain unchanged despite the additional appendix evidence.

C2.justification: v4 adds substantive explanations for weak SD3.5 transfer, limited benefits from combining VAEs, linear-probing and ResNet difficulties, and DINO-versus-CLIP performance. Appendix F interprets regional score variation as spatially uneven artifacts. The limitations discussion additionally addresses smartphone enhancement artifacts and ambiguity in the real/synthetic boundary, extending v1's post-processing limitation.

D1.justification: v1 provides a short setup and refers to an appendix absent from the supplied PDF. v4 discloses eight V100 GPUs, learning rate 1e-4, batch size 16, 32-step gradient accumulation, evaluation every 2,500 iterations and an early-stopping criterion. It also identifies the DINOv2 ViT-L/14 configuration and documents EvalGEN's 553 prompts, 20 images per prompt per generator and JPEG-96 storage. These are substantial documentation additions.

R1.justification: The same 42 referenced works and main related-work positioning are retained. Appendix B expands descriptions of existing peers, while Appendices C–D add targeted contrasts concerning the ForenSynth baselines' training-domain exposure and DDA's backbone requirements relative to AlignedForensics.

P1.justification: The main section order and most prose remain intact. v4 rewrites the misaligned-dataset explanation, edits captions and limitations, updates the author/affiliation presentation and adds organized Appendices A–F. Most expansion documents additional evidence rather than extensively rewriting the existing narrative.

P2.justification: v4 adds the decision-boundary diagram, expanded detector-feature visualization, EvalGEN image grid and regional heatmaps (Figures 3 and 11–13), plus Tables 11–17, including a consolidated benchmark overview. Existing figures are cropped or rescaled and tables redistributed. v1 Figures 3–9 correspond to v4 Figures 4–10 rather than being removed.

improvement.justification: The appendix substantially fills v1's gaps in implementation documentation and evidence supporting backbone and input-size choices. Added benchmark comparisons also expose weaker ForenSynth performance, making generalization limits more visible. Reporting problems temper these gains: ForenSynth's DDA standard deviation is 8.9 in Table 11 but 0.9 in Table 13, and Appendix A leaves the separation of early stopping from benchmark evaluation unclear. Nevertheless, the additional reproducibility information and diagnostic evidence provide a substantial net improvement.
